body_markdown:
Restoring vintage cars—or simply keeping project cars functional and on the road—can be challenging. For one thing, the older a car gets, the fewer new-old stock (NOS) parts are available. Even cars built in this century may use parts that are difficult to come by. Luckily, technology is helping bridge the gap by making it easier to design and manufacture at least some of these impossible-to-source parts. Digital 3D models can be used to print interior pieces in various plastics. You can order sheetmetal brackets from multiple retailers that have laser-cut them and bent them to spec. Now that metal 3D printing is becoming more and more widespread, the possibilities are expanding, and prices are coming down.


To learn about the current state of 3D printing that’s available to consumers, I decided to first learn one of the more popular modeling software platforms available,[Autodesk Fusion](https://www.autodesk.com/products/fusion-360/overview) . Formerly Fusion 360, and often jokingly referred to as Confusion 360 because of its complexity, the software has a lot of very intuitive tools and some that are appropriately complex. For the home hobbyist, the software is free, and that has helped it grow far and wide in all sorts of DIY communities. Here are some of the lessons I’ve learned in five or six weeks, as someone who hasn’t tried computer-aided design (CAD) software in about 25 years.


## It’s Easy to Learn a Lot, Quickly


It’s simple, but it’s a start. About 20 minutes after firing up Fusion and watching a tutorial, you can be on your way to duplicating parts in 3D.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


I shouldn’t have been surprised that there are so many resources out there to learn one of the most powerful and accessible CAD programs available. There are several tutorials available that help newbies like myself. I made it about 10 days into the[Learn Autodesk Fusion in 30 Days](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4G2E_DqQteM) tutorial on YouTube before I was champing at the bit to start my own projects. The software is so powerful. While there is a bit of a learning curve, once you get a grasp of the most basic tools, the possibilities of what you can model start to expand rapidly. (I really need to go back and finish the last few lessons in that course. If I had done so when I started, I would have saved myself a lot of trouble.)


## You Won’t Be the First to Have That Problem


This is really an extension of the last point. Still, beyond all the beginner tutorials out there, a simple search for a very specific problem will probably turn up several videos or forum posts that walk you through the solution. It seems like there’s always more than one way to model something.


## 3D Space Can Be a Brainteaser


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


I’ve had several designs turn out to be far more difficult than I’d anticipated. It turns out that my brain is a bit optimistic when conceiving complex 3D parts with close tolerances. When you’re working on a hobby project, the challenge of cramming the geometry into a confined space can be a bit of a game. I’ve had to be pried away from my laptop more than once when I felt compelled to figure out a tough issue. Still, seeing something you’ve conceived in your mind become a realistic-looking 3D model is always fun.


## Garbage In, Garbage Out


Your 3D model is only as accurate as you design it to be. When trying to match a part to a project, careful measurements are critical. A couple of rulers, a straightedge, and a protractor can take out the guesswork. A 3D scanner would also be helpful, although those are still on the pricey side for the average enthusiast. Just don’t jump to conclusions. I made a mistake when measuring on a project and built to tolerances that were too generous because I discovered way too late that an interfering part I was designing around was not perpendicular to a surface, but angled 3 degrees.


## Cheat Whenever You Can


Screenshot


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


MSD offers cross sections of many of its distributors with dimensions. It’s enough to get the basics and render them quickly.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Maybe you need to measure and model a part, and maybe you don’t. If your model relies on bits of hardware and you need to make sure they fit and don’t interfere, you could spend quite a lot of time sourcing, measuring, and designing them in 3D, or you could just import the models from someone who has already done all the tedious work. McMaster-Carr has close to a million parts for sale, and you’d be surprised how many of them are available in several 3D and 2D formats.


Further, many mechanical parts you might want to render can be found on product websites along with dimensions or scans that can be imported into Fusion and traced to get you started. That goes for gaskets, which can be a great place to start, as well as lots of mechanical parts you may need to render to check for space constraints: intake manifolds, valve covers, distributors. . .


## Going Back in Time Can Have Big Consequences


Fusion warns you every time there’s an error with red or yellow shading over the actions in the timeline. In this case, a lot of them popped up in the timeline in close succession.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


One of the great aspects of 3D modeling is that you can virtually go back in time to an earlier part of your project and change a dimension or insert a new action. If you plan ahead, changing the timeline to swap the order of operations of an action can eliminate repetitive modeling tasks and save a lot of time. However, *Back to the Future* , *Terminator 2* , and *Primer* all should have prepared me for the trouble that can arise with time travel.


Going back and changing something early on in the process can cause big problems downstream when reference surfaces get moved or deleted, or when several parts get combined into a single 3D body. This is yet another reason why it’s imperative to get things right when you’re building the early sketches that lay the foundation for your project.


All in all, I’d recommend Autodesk Fusion to anyone looking to expand their DIY skill sets. It opens up a lot of possibilities for one-off part production, especially if your coworker promises to use any shift knob you design on[their LS-swapped Corvette](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/my-corvette-had-a-rough-first-go-at-the-track-and-im-not-even-mad/) .


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)
